segments.caption: In 1908, a brewer at Guinness had a problem: he could only test a few batches at a time.
With so little data, the normal curve made him too confident.
His fix is the t-distribution.
Here's the definition, in simple words.
The t-distribution looks like the normal bell curve, but with fatter tails.
We use it when the sample is small, and we have to guess the spread from the data itself.
The smaller the sample, the fatter the tails.
Why fatter tails? Because with only a few values, our guess of the spread is shaky.
Take five values, and the spread can look small one time, and big the next.
Fatter tails leave room for that extra uncertainty.
Its exact shape depends on one number: the degrees of freedom.
Usually, that's the sample size, minus one. So five values give four degrees of freedom.
With four degrees of freedom, the tails are fat.
With ten, they slim down.
And by about thirty, the t-curve is almost exactly the normal curve.
Why does this matter? Think about the middle 95%.
On the normal curve, it stretches about two steps from the centre.
But with only five values, the t-curve needs about 2.8 steps.
So small samples give wider, more honest ranges.
So remember: the t-distribution is a bell with fatter tails, for small samples.
The bigger the sample, the closer it gets to normal.
Quick quiz!
Imagine collecting more and more data.
As the sample grows, what does the t-distribution turn into?
The normal distribution!
With more data, the extra uncertainty fades, and the tails slim down to the normal curve.
Next: is this dice fair? The chi-square distribution.
Follow for data science made simple!
